items.name: Shah Alam II
items.desc: Shah Alam II — medieval India, 1728–1806.
items.note: Shah Alam II , also known by his birth name Ali Gohar, or Ali Gauhar, was the seventeenth Mughal emperor and the son of Alamgir II. The reign of Shah Alam saw a number of invasions, the first and foremost by Ahmed Shah Abdali in 1761, which led to the third battle of Panipat between the Maratha Empire and the Afghans under Abdali. The invading forces of Abdali then drove out the Marathas led by Sadashivrao Bhau, deposed Shah Jahan III, the puppet Mughal emperor of Imad-ul-Mulk, and installed Shah Alam II as the rightful emperor.

He was placed in power in September 1843, at the age of five, with his mother ruling on his behalf, and after their defeat in the Anglo-Sikh War, under a British Resident.

items.note: Rajgir is an ancient city and university town in the Nalanda district of Bihar, India. Other historical figures such as Mahavira and king Bimbisara lived there, and due to its religious significance, the city holds a place of prominence in Buddhist, Jain and Hindu scriptures.

The capital is Malé, one of the most densely populated cities in the world. The Maldives is at the forefront of climate change vulnerability, facing existential threat from sea level rise. The archipelago is home to unique coral reef ecosystems with over 1,000 fish species.

Aurangzeb and the Mughals belonged to a branch of the Timurid dynasty.

items.name: Akbar
items.desc: Akbar — medieval India, 1542–1605.
items.note: Akbar 15 October 1542 – 27 October 1605), also known as Akbar the Great, was the third Mughal emperor, who reigned from 1556 to 1605. items.name: Ashoka
items.desc: Ashoka — ancient, 304 BCE–232 BCE.
items.note: Ashoka, also known as Asoka or Aśoka, most commonly known as Ashoka the Great, was Emperor of Magadha from c. 268 BCE until his death, and the third ruler from the Mauryan dynasty. His empire covered a large part of the Indian subcontinent, stretching from present-day Afghanistan in the west to present-day Bangladesh in the east, with its capital at Pataliputra.

items.name: Bajirao I

items.name: Humayun

At the time of his death, the Mughal Empire spanned almost one million square kilometers. On 26 December 1530, Humayun succeeded his father Babur to the throne of Delhi as ruler of the Mughal territories in the Indian subcontinent.

items.desc: ancient defensive wall across northern China
items.note: The Great Wall of China is a series of fortifications built across the northern borders of China to protect against invasions. Construction began as early as the 7th century BC, with the most famous sections built by the Ming Dynasty (1368-1644). The wall stretches over 21,000 km, making it the longest man-made structure in the world. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and one of the New Seven Wonders of the World. The wall features watchtowers, garrison stations, and beacon towers. Contrary to popular belief, the wall is not visible from space with the naked eye. It attracts over 10 million visitors annually, with the most popular section near Beijing at Badaling.

items.desc: Hyder Ali — medieval India, 1722–1782.

items.name: Shah Alam II
items.desc: Shah Alam II — medieval India, 1728–1806.
items.note: Shah Alam II , also known by his birth name Ali Gohar, or Ali Gauhar, was the seventeenth Mughal emperor and the son of Alamgir II. The reign of Shah Alam saw a number of invasions, the first and foremost by Ahmed Shah Abdali in 1761, which led to the third battle of Panipat between the Maratha Empire and the Afghans under Abdali. The invading forces of Abdali then drove out the Marathas led by Sadashivrao Bhau, deposed Shah Jahan III, the puppet Mughal emperor of Imad-ul-Mulk, and installed Shah Alam II as the rightful emperor.

items.name: Bahadur Shah Zafar
items.desc: Bahadur Shah Zafar — medieval India, 1775–1862.
items.note: Bahadur Shah II , also known by his poetic title Bahadur Shah Zafar , was the twentieth and last Mughal emperor and an Urdu poet. He was a titular emperor with his authority limited to the Walled City of Delhi, but was declared the Emperor of India by the forces opposing East India Company forces in parts of the Indian subcontinent during the Indian Rebellion of 1857. Zafar was exiled to Yangon in British-controlled Burma in December 1857 by the East India Company after rebel defeat in the war, putting an end to the nearly 500-year long Timurid dynasty started by Timur.

items.name: Kushan Empire

items.note: The Kushan Empire was a syncretic empire formed by the Yuezhi in the Bactrian territories in the early 1st century. It spread to encompass much of what is now Afghanistan, India, Pakistan, Nepal, Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. Kushan territory in India went at least as far as Saketa and Sarnath, now near Varanasi in Uttar Pradesh, where inscriptions have been found dating to the era of the Kushan emperor Kanishka the Great.

items.name: Maldives
items.note: The Maldives is an archipelago nation of 26 coral atolls in the Indian Ocean, comprising about 1,190 islands, of which 200 are inhabited. It is the lowest-lying country in the world with an average ground level of 1.5 meters above sea level. The islands are known for their stunning white-sand beaches, crystal-clear lagoons, and world-class scuba diving. The economy is almost entirely dependent on tourism and fishing. The capital is Malé, one of the most densely populated cities in the world. The Maldives is at the forefront of climate change vulnerability, facing existential threat from sea level rise. The archipelago is home to unique coral reef ecosystems with over 1,000 fish species.

items.name: Akbar
items.desc: Akbar — medieval India, 1542–1605.
items.note: Akbar 15 October 1542 – 27 October 1605), also known as Akbar the Great, was the third Mughal emperor, who reigned from 1556 to 1605. Akbar succeeded his father, Humayun, under a regent, Bairam Khan, who helped the young emperor expand and consolidate Mughal domains in the Indian subcontinent. He is generally considered one of the greatest Mughal emperors.

items.name: Aurangzeb
items.desc: Aurangzeb — medieval India, 1618–1707.
items.note: Alamgir I , commonly known by the title Aurangzeb, was the sixth Mughal emperor, reigning from 1658 until his death in 1707. Under his reign, the Mughal Empire reached its greatest extent, with territory spanning nearly the entirety of the Indian subcontinent. Aurangzeb and the Mughals belonged to a branch of the Timurid dynasty.

items.name: Babur
items.desc: founder of the Mughal Empire
items.note: Babur's cousin, Mirza Haidar asserted that the armies might have numbered over 200,000 troops

items.name: Shah Jahan
items.desc: Mughal emperor who built the Taj Mahal
items.note: Shah Jahan I , also called Shah Jahan the Magnificent, was the fifth Mughal Emperor from 1628 until his deposition in 1658. His reign marked the zenith of Mughal architectural and cultural achievements. The third son of Jahangir , Shah Jahan participated in the military campaigns against the Sisodia Rajputs of Mewar and the rebel Lodi nobles of the Deccan.

items.name: Humayun
items.desc: Humayun — medieval India, 1508–1556.
items.note: Nasir al-Din Muhammad , commonly known by his regnal name Humayun , was the second Mughal emperor, who ruled much of what is now eastern Afghanistan, Bangladesh, Northern India, and Pakistan from 1530 to 1540 and again from 1555 to his death in 1556. At the time of his death, the Mughal Empire spanned almost one million square kilometers. On 26 December 1530, Humayun succeeded his father Babur to the throne of Delhi as ruler of the Mughal territories in the Indian subcontinent.

items.name: Jahangir
items.desc: Jahangir — medieval India, 1569–1627.
items.note: Nur ud-din Muhammad Salim , known by his royal name Jahangir , was the fourth emperor of the Mughal Empire, reigning from 1605 until his death in 1627. The third and only surviving son of Emperor Akbar I and his consort Maryam uz-Zamani. Jahangir received a comprehensive education, which included the languages Chagatai, Persian, and Hindustani, as well as diverse subjects such as military tactics and social sciences.

items.name: Shah Alam II
items.desc: Shah Alam II — medieval India, 1728–1806.
items.note: Shah Alam II , also known by his birth name Ali Gohar, or Ali Gauhar, was the seventeenth Mughal emperor and the son of Alamgir II. The reign of Shah Alam saw a number of invasions, the first and foremost by Ahmed Shah Abdali in 1761, which led to the third battle of Panipat between the Maratha Empire and the Afghans under Abdali. The invading forces of Abdali then drove out the Marathas led by Sadashivrao Bhau, deposed Shah Jahan III, the puppet Mughal emperor of Imad-ul-Mulk, and installed Shah Alam II as the rightful emperor.

branches.title: Geography
branches.desc: The physical geography of the Iberian Peninsula and Spain's territory.

items.name: Iberian Peninsula
items.desc: The peninsula at the south-west of Europe, holding Spain and Portugal; separated from the rest of Europe by the Pyrenees.

items.name: Pyrenees
items.desc: Mountain range forming the natural border between Spain and France, extending from the Bay of Biscay to the Mediterranean.

items.name: Meseta Central
items.desc: The high plateau basin occupying central Spain, ringed by the Cantabrian, Iberian and Betic ranges.

items.name: Strait of Gibraltar
items.desc: The narrow waterway between southern Spain and North Africa, linking the Mediterranean with the Atlantic.

items.name: Ebro River
items.desc: The longest river wholly in Spain, flowing from the Cantabrian Mountains to the Mediterranean delta in Aragon.

items.name: Tagus River
items.desc: The river running across the Meseta through Madrid and Toledo to Lisbon, forming part of the Spain–Portugal border.

items.name: Guadalquivir River
items.desc: The main river of Andalusia, flowing through Seville and Cadiz to the Atlantic; gives its name to Guadalquivir.

items.name: Balearic Islands
items.desc: The island group of Majorca, Menorca, Ibiza and Formentera in the western Mediterranean, part of Spain.

items.name: Canary Islands
items.desc: Spanish Atlantic archipelago off north-west Africa; the largest, Tenerife, holds Mount Teide.

items.name: Ceuta
items.desc: Spanish autonomous city and port at the Strait of Gibraltar, forming a land border with Morocco.

items.name: Melilla
items.desc: Spanish autonomous city and port on the North African coast, forming a land border with Morocco.

branches.title: Ancient
branches.desc: Pre-Roman peoples and the Roman conquest of Hispania.

items.name: Iberians
items.desc: Pre-Roman people of the eastern and southern Iberian Peninsula, absorbed by Rome by the 1st century BC.

items.name: Celts
items.desc: Iron Age Celtic-speaking peoples who settled much of the peninsula before the Roman conquest.

items.name: Phoenicians
items.desc: Maritime traders from Tyre who founded colonies including Cadiz, the oldest continuously inhabited city in Spain.

items.name: Carthage
items.desc: Carthaginian maritime power in North Africa; established Gades (Cadiz) and Ebusus (Ibiza) and fought Rome for control of Hispania.

items.name: Hannibal
items.desc: Carthaginian general whose 218-201 BC Italian campaign began the Second Punic War.

items.name: Second Punic War
items.desc: 218-201 BC war in which Carthage under Hannibal contested Roman control of Hispania, ending in Roman victory.

items.name: Roman Hispania
items.desc: Roman Spain after the conquest completed by 19 BC; divided into Tarraconensis, Baetica and Lusitania.

branches.title: Medieval
branches.desc: Visigothic, Muslim and Christian polities in medieval Iberia.

items.name: Visigothic Kingdom
items.desc: Germanic kingdom ruling most of Iberia from the 6th century, overthrown by the Umayyads in 711-718.

items.name: Tariq ibn Ziyad
items.desc: Umayyad commander whose 711 victory at Guadalete opened the Muslim conquest of Hispania; Gibraltar takes its name from Jabal Tariq.

items.name: Muslim Conquest of Hispania
items.desc: 711-718 Umayyad invasion that ended the Visigothic Kingdom and established al-Andalus.

items.name: Al-Andalus
items.desc: The Muslim-ruled territories of the Iberian Peninsula from 711 to the fall of Granada in 1492.

items.name: Umayyad Emirate of Córdoba
items.desc: 756-929 polity founded by Abd al-Rahman I after the Abbasid overthrow of his dynasty, seat of the Andalusi caliphal court.

items.name: Caliphate of Córdoba
items.desc: 929-1031 caliphate under Abd al-Rahman III and successors, marking the political and cultural high point of al-Andalus.

items.name: Abd al-Rahman I
items.desc: Umayyad prince who founded the emirate of Cordoba in 756 after escaping the Abbasid massacre of his family.

items.name: Abd al-Rahman III
items.desc: Emir who proclaimed the caliphate in 929 at Medina Azahara and defeated Charles the Bald at Simancas in 939.

items.name: Taifa Kingdoms
items.desc: Post-1031 successor states of the caliphate, divided among multiple Muslim rulers, before being pushed south by Castile and Aragon.

items.name: Almoravids
items.desc: Almohad-era confederation of Berber dynasties from the western Sahara that ruled al-Andalus in the 11th-12th centuries.

items.name: Almohads
items.desc: Berber dynasty that replaced the Almoravids in al-Andalus and pushed the frontier south of the Tagus by 1170.

items.name: Reconquista
items.desc: The centuries-long Christian conquest of al-Andalus, conventionally dated from Covadonga in 718 to the fall of Granada in 1492.

items.name: Castile
items.desc: Christian kingdom of northern Iberia, the main agent of the Reconquista and later the core of Spain.

items.name: Aragon
items.desc: Kingdom in the north-east that joined Castile in 1479 and brought the Mediterranean and Catalan-Aragonese lands into the union.

items.name: Leon
items.desc: Asturian successor kingdom whose Cortes of Leon in 1188 are often cited as the origin of the Spanish Cortes.

items.name: Navarre
items.desc: Kingdom on the Pyrenean western frontier that remained independent while Castile and Aragon expanded south.

items.name: Nasrid Kingdom of Granada
items.desc: The last Muslim state in Iberia, ruled by the Nasrid dynasty from the Alhambra at Granada until 1492.

branches.title: 15th-16th Century
branches.desc: The dynastic union of Castile and Aragon and the first Spanish empire.

items.name: Isabella I of Castile
items.desc: Queen of Castile from 1474, who married Ferdinand of Aragon and completed the unification of Spain and launched the Columbus voyages.

items.name: Ferdinand II of Aragon
items.desc: King of Aragon from 1479, co-ruler with Isabella; their marriage founded the united Spanish monarchy.

items.name: Union of Castile and Aragon
items.desc: 1479 dynastic union of the two crowns, conventionally the birth of modern Spain; the crowns remained legally distinct.

items.name: Fall of Granada
items.desc: 1492 surrender of the Nasrid Kingdom of Granada to Ferdinand and Isabella, ending the Reconquista.

items.name: Christopher Columbus
items.desc: Genoese navigator who sailed from Palos in 1492 and reached the Caribbean, opening Spanish involvement in the Americas.

items.name: Voyages of Columbus
items.desc: Four Atlantic voyages of 1492-1504 that began sustained European contact with the Americas.

items.name: Spanish Empire
items.desc: The overseas and European possessions of the Spanish monarchy, at its height spanning the Americas, the Philippines and parts of Europe and Africa.

items.name: Charles I
items.desc: Charles V of Spain, grandson of Ferdinand and Isabella, who became Holy Roman Emperor in 1519 and inherited the Habsburg lands.

items.name: Charles V
items.desc: Holy Roman Emperor and king of Spain, whose reign saw the Reformation, the conquest of Peru and the 1520s Mediterranean conflict with France and the Ottomans.

items.name: Philip II
items.desc: King of Spain 1556-1598, the most powerful monarch of his age, who saw the conquest of Portugal, the Spanish Armada and the Escorial.

items.name: Spanish Armada
items.desc: The 1588 Spanish fleet sent to escort Philip II's forces to England, defeated by the English and storms.

branches.title: 17th-18th Century
branches.desc: Habsburg and Bourbon Spain after the Golden Age.

items.name: Habsburg Spain
items.desc: The Spanish Habsburg period (1516-1700), the great imperial and cultural peak ending in catastrophe with the War of the Spanish Succession.

items.name: War of the Spanish Succession
items.desc: 1701-1714 war over the disputed Bourbon succession to the Spanish throne, settled at Utrecht with Philip V recognised.

items.name: Philip V
items.desc: First Bourbon king of Spain, 1700-1724 and again 1724-1746; his accession triggered the War of the Spanish Succession.

items.name: Bourbon Spain
items.desc: The Bourbon dynasty and its reforms in 18th-century Spain, which strengthened the crown and weakened the aristocracy.

items.name: Bourbon Reforms
items.desc: 18th-century centralising and modernising reforms of the Bourbon monarchy under the ilustrados.

branches.title: 19th Century
branches.desc: Peninsular occupation, constitutional experiments and the loss of the colonies.

items.name: Peninsular War
items.desc: 1808-1814 Napoleonic occupation of Spain, begun when French troops deposed the Bourbons and resisted by guerrilla warfare.

items.name: Napoleon Bonaparte
items.desc: French emperor who invaded Spain in 1808 and made his brother Joseph king, triggering prolonged Peninsular resistance.

items.name: Joseph Bonaparte
items.desc: Napoleon's brother, installed as king of Spain in 1808 and never accepted by the Spanish; the Jiufe independence began in his name.

items.name: Cadiz Constitution 1812
items.desc: Spain's first constitution, drafted in Cadiz and never fully enacted; proclaimed liberal sovereignty and national citizenship.

items.name: Ferdinand VII
items.desc: King restored in 1814, who abolished the Cadiz Constitution and ruled into the liberal revolutions of 1820-23 and 1830s.

items.name: Carlist Wars
items.desc: 1833-1849 civil wars in which the Carlist pretender fought successive liberal governments over the Spanish succession.

items.name: First Spanish Republic
items.desc: The republic proclaimed in 1873, which lasted eleven months before Bourbon restoration.

items.name: Spanish-American War
items.desc: 1898 war in which Spain lost Cuba, Puerto Rico, the Philippines and Guam to the United States, ending the Spanish empire.

branches.title: 20th Century
branches.desc: Republic, civil war and the Franco dictatorship.

items.name: Second Spanish Republic
items.desc: The republic of 1931-1939 that followed the 1931 local elections and preceded the civil war.

items.name: Spanish Civil War
items.desc: 1936-1939 conflict between the Nationalists under Franco and the Republican government, with German, Italian and Soviet involvement.

items.name: Francisco Franco
items.desc: Nationalist leader who won the civil war and ruled as dictator of Spain from 1939 until his death in 1975.

items.name: Francoist Spain
items.desc: The Franco dictatorship from 1939, marked by censorship, economic opening after 1959 and gradual normalisation in the 1960s-70s.

items.name: Guernica
items.desc: Basque town bombed in 1937 by German and Italian aircraft supporting the Nationalists; later painted by Picasso.

items.name: Pablo Picasso
items.desc: Spanish painter whose Guernica is the best-known image of the Spanish Civil War.

items.name: Democratic Transition
items.title: Democratic Transition
items.desc: The 1975-1982 shift from Franco's dictatorship to a parliamentary monarchy, marked by the 1978 Constitution.

items.name: Juan Carlos I
items.desc: King of Spain 1975-2014, chosen by Franco and the first monarch of the restored monarchy who presided over the transition.

items.name: Adolfo Suarez
items.desc: Prime Minister 1976-1981 who steered the transition, founded the UCD and carried the 1978 Constitution through the Cortes.

items.name: Constitution of Spain 1978
items.desc: The constitution of the Spanish state, establishing the parliamentary monarchy, the autonomous communities and the Catalan and Basque co-official languages.

branches.title: Modern
branches.desc: Present-day Spanish institutions, membership and economy.

items.name: Parliamentary Monarchy
items.desc: The form of government since 1975: the king is head of state and ceremonial, with legislative power in the Cortes Generales.

items.name: Cortes Generales
items.desc: The Spanish parliament, comprising the Congress of Deputies and the Senate; the Congress was first convened in 1188 at Leon.

items.name: Congress of Deputies
items.desc: The lower house of the Spanish parliament, whose 350 members are elected by proportional representation.

items.name: Senate of Spain
items.desc: The upper house of the Spanish parliament, composed of elected members plus members appointed by the autonomous communities.

items.name: Autonomous Communities
items.desc: The seventeen autonomous communities created under the 1978 Constitution, each with its own statute, parliament and government.

items.name: European Union
items.desc: The European Union, which Spain joined on 1 January 1986.

items.name: NATO
items.desc: The North Atlantic Treaty Organization, which Spain joined in 1982, a late accession reflecting its neutrality under Franco.

items.name: Spain-EU accession
items.desc: Spain joined the European Economic Community and the European Communities on 1 January 1986 after years of negotiation.

items.name: Spanish economy
items.desc: The economy of Spain, the eurozone's fourth largest, built on services, tourism, automotive manufacturing and agriculture.
